audit.recode_to: naga1394: not fixed / weight-sensitive — primary stress on the final syllable when it is closed (polysyllables), on a diphthong where present, otherwise on the first syllable (monosyllables, open-final disyllables); cite Baishya 2004 ch.4 sec.4.10.1 pp.119-120; remove from fixed-strict and dominant-initial sets; family Indo-European (Assamese-lexified creole) stays. the StressTyp2 entry for this language datum ('initial, all words', sourced only to Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader) -> tang1336, Sino-Tibetan, survey-only/source-not-located (Arokianathan 1987 and Khuraijam 2014 describe Tangkhul as a 3-tone language and state no word-stress rule).

sources.citation: Arokianathan, S. 1987. Tangkhul-Naga Grammar (A Study of Word Formation). CIIL Grammar Series 16. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. (CIIL e-book HTML,http://www.ciil-ebooks.net/html/tangkhul/)
sources.quote: sec. 1.0: 'There are 7 vowels and 21 consonants in Tangkhul-Naga. As suprasegmental features, there are tones, length and nasality.' sec. 1.7: 'Tangkhul-Naga is a tone language having lexically significant, contrastive, but relative pitch on each syllable. ... There are three level tonemes and two gliding tonemes in the language.' No word-stress placement rule anywhere in the chapter.
